title: What should post-training optimize? A test-time scaling law perspective

paper.title: What should post-training optimize? A test-time scaling law perspective
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models are increasingly deployed with test-time strategies: sample N N responses, score them with a reward model or verifier, and return the best. This deployment rule exposes a mismatch in post-training: standard objectives optimize the mean reward of a single response, whereas best-of- N N performance is governed by the upper tail of the reward distribution. Recent test-time-aware objectives partly address this mismatch, but typically assume that training can use the same per-prompt rollout budget as deployment, which is impractical when post-training must cover many prompts while deployment can allocate much larger per-prompt test-time compute. We study this budget-mismatch regime, where only m ≪ N m\ll N per-prompt rollouts are available during training but the target objective is best-of- N N deployment. Under structural assumptions on the reward tails, we show that the policy gradient of the best-of- N N objective can be approximated from a much smaller rollout group by extrapolating upper-tail statistics. This yields a family of Tail-Extrapolated estimators for best-of- N N -oriented post-training: a simple direct estimator, Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA), and a fixed-order debiased Prefix-TEA estimator based on moment cancellation. Experiments on instruction-following tasks show that TEA and Prefix-TEA improve best-of- N N performance across different language models, reward models and datasets under various training and test-time budget settings.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The modern workflow for large language models (LLM) typically consists of three stages: pre-training, post-training, and test-time adaptation. Post-training is a critical stage in the development of large language models (LLMs), where a pre-trained model is further fine-tuned using reinforcement learning to optimize a task-specific objective or align with human preferences. At deployment time, practitioners often use additional test-time compute to improve performance. A widely used strategy is best-of- N N sampling: for each prompt, one draws N N independent responses from the model, scores them with a reward model, and returns the one with the largest score. This test-time strategy can substantially improve performance, but it also creates a mismatch with the standard post-training objective, which optimizes the expected reward of a single response rather than the best response among N N samples. This mismatch is not only conceptually unsatisfying, but also practically sub-optimal. Empirically, reward-guided fine-tuning has been shown to reduce output diversity across different tasks, which removes precisely the stochasticity that the best-of- N N (BoN) sampling strategy relies on ( Kirk et al., 2023 ; O’Mahony et al., 2024 ) . Direct test-time-aware training studies give complementary evidence: BoN-aware, pass@ k k /majority-vote-aware, and max@ k k objectives improve best-of- N N or set-level performance on various benchmarks over standard single-sample objectives ( Chow et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Bagirov et al., 2025 ; Ousherovitch and Tewari, 2026 ) . These test-time-aware post-training methods typically involve computing the test-time objective directly during training, which requires a large rollout budget per prompt. For example, if the test-time strategy is best-of- N N sampling, then for each prompt during training, one needs to generate at least N N responses to compute the objective and the policy gradient. This matched-budget requirement creates tension between post-training and test-time deployment. On the one hand, post-training must cover a large number of prompts, so the rollout budget available for each individual prompt is often limited ( Zhang and Zuo, 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . On the other hand, test-time compute is increasingly treated as a separate scaling dimension, and recent work has begun to study deployment regimes with substantially larger search budgets ( Snell et al., 2024 ; Chow et al., 2024 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . This motivates the key question: Can we optimize best-of- N N performance when only m ≪ N m\ll N rollouts per prompt are available during training? In this paper, we provide a solution to this question through the lens of test-time scaling laws , which characterize how best-of- N N performance scales with N N under a given policy. Recently, Li et al., Li et al. (2026) characterize the BoN scaling law by modeling the upper tail of the reward distribution, and show that the BoN scaling law can be predicted using m ≪ N m\ll N samples by extrapolating upper-tail statistics. Drawing on this perspective, we develop a family of algorithms that use tail extrapolation to optimize best-of- N N performance under a small rollout budget. Our main contributions are as follows: • We derive a class of Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA) estimators for the advantage function and policy gradient of the best-of- N N objective, which can be estimated from m ≪ N m\ll N rollouts per prompt. We further construct a debiased estimator, Prefix-TEA, which further removes the bias in stochastic gradient estimation. • We prove non-asymptotic gradient estimation error bounds for TEA and Prefix-TEA, characterizing the bias–variance tradeoff and the dependence on the training budget m m and the test-time budget N N . Building upon these guarantees, we establish convergence guarantees for post-training with TEA and Prefix-TEA, with respect to the best-of- N N objective. • We conduct extensive experiments on instruction-following tasks, showing that TEA and Prefix-TEA consistently improve best-of- N N performance over GRPO and recent test-time-aware baselines across datasets and reward models under various training and test-time budget settings. We provide a detailed discussion of related work in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 2.2 From standard post-training to test-time-aware training
sections.text: In standard RLHF-style post-training, the policy is optimized to improve the expected reward while staying close to a reference policy. Concretely, the training objective takes the form J RN ( θ ) := 𝔼 x ∼ P X [ 𝔼 y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ R ( x , y ) ] − β KL ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ∥ π ref ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ) ] . J_{\mathrm{RN}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{X}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[R(x,y)\bigr]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\Bigr]. (2) This objective is driven by the mean reward under the current policy. At deployment time, however, one often uses additional test-time compute, for example through best-of- N N sampling: for each prompt x x , one draws N N independent responses from π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , scores them with the reward model, and returns the one with the largest score. This induces the promptwise value V N ( θ ; x ) := 𝔼 [ max 1 ⩽ i ⩽ N R ( x , y i ) | x , y 1 , … , y N ∼ i . i . d . π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ] . V_{N}(\theta;x):=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\max_{1\leqslant i\leqslant N}R(x,y_{i})\,\Bigm|\,x,\;y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\Bigr]. (3) Therefore, if the goal of post-training is to improve performance under some additional test-time budget, a natural objective is J TT ( θ ) := 𝔼 x ∼ P X [ V N ( θ ; x ) − β KL ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ∥ π ref ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ) ] . J_{\mathrm{TT}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{X}}\Bigl[V_{N}(\theta;x)-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)\Bigr]. (4) The difference between ( 2 ) and ( 4 ) is the part of the reward distribution being optimized. Mean-reward post-training improves the average sample, whereas best-of- N N deployment is controlled by the upper tail. Directly optimizing ( 4 ) with a matched budget would require rollout groups comparable to the deployment budget N N . In modern post-training, this is often impractical: the training rollout budget per prompt is limited, while deployment may use a much larger search budget. We therefore focus on the finite-budget regime m ≪ N , m\ll N, and ask how to construct a test-time-aware training signal from only m m rollouts per prompt.

sections.heading: Fixed-order debiasing.
sections.text: In Appendix D.5 , we construct a cross-fitted plug-in estimator that admits a finite expansion in inverse powers of the rollout budget. Then there exist constants C , c > 0 C,c>0 , depending only on ( α , G , σ min , M R ) (\alpha,G,\sigma_{\min},M_{R}) , and in the fixed-order case also on the fixed pair ( k , J ) (k,J) , such that for every 0 < γ ⩽ c 1 + β + log ⁡ N , 0<\gamma\leqslant\frac{c}{1+\beta+\sqrt{\log N}}, and all sufficiently large m m , 1 T ​ ∑ t = 0 T − 1 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ ∇ θ J ^ TT ​ ( θ t ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ⁡ [ J ^ TT ⋆ − J ^ TT ​ ( θ 0 ) γ ​ T + 𝖡 m + γ ​ log ⁡ N + β 2 P ] , \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\left\|\nabla_{\theta}\widehat{J}_{\mathrm{TT}}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}\Big]\leqslant C\Big[\frac{\widehat{J}_{\mathrm{TT}}^{\star}-\widehat{J}_{\mathrm{TT}}(\theta_{0})}{\gamma T}+\mathsf{B}_{m}+\gamma\frac{\log N+\beta^{2}}{P}\Big], (14) where 𝖡 m = log ⁡ N / m 2 \mathsf{B}_{m}=\log N/m^{2} for the direct plug-in estimator ( 11 ), and 𝖡 m = log ⁡ N / m 2 ​ k \mathsf{B}_{m}=\log N/m^{2k} for the fixed-order estimator in Theorem 2 . Remark 1 . Fixed-order debiasing reduces the systematic finite-rollout bias, but its constant depends on ( k , J ) (k,J) . Thus fixed-order debiasing is most useful when the rollout budget m m and prompt batch P P are large enough for the smaller bias floor to outweigh the additional constant costs. Appendix E isolates this frontier in a controlled Gaussian-tail simulation. In the next section, we implement our finite-rollout gradient estimators in a realistic post-training pipeline and test whether they improve best-of- N N performance with a small per-prompt rollout budget.

sections.heading: Training interface.
sections.text: The estimators in Section 3 define promptwise updates of the form g ^ x ​ ( A ) = 1 m ​ ∑ i = 1 m A i ​ ∇ θ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y i ∣ x ) . \widehat{g}_{x}(A)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x). In experiments, we use this form as the common training interface. For each prompt x x , the current policy samples m m responses, the reward model assigns rewards R i = R ⁡ ( x , y i ) R_{i}=R(x,y_{i}) , and each method computes a scalar advantage A i A_{i} from this reward group. We then use A i A_{i} as stop-gradient advantage weights in the same grouped on-policy training pipeline with KL regularization. Thus all methods share the rollout budget, reward model, log-probability computation, KL penalty, optimizer, and checkpoint selection rule; they differ only in how they construct A i A_{i} .

sections.heading: TEA estimators.
sections.text: Section 3 defines two finite-rollout gradient estimators. We call the advantage induced by the direct plug-in estimator Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA). The direct plug-in estimator in Eq. ( 11 ) already has the score-function form g ^ m dir ( θ ; x ) = 1 m ∑ i = 1 m A i raw S θ ( x , y i ) , A i raw = 1 α 𝕀 { R i ⩾ r ^ m } R ~ η ^ m ( R i ) , \widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}(\theta;x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_{i}^{\mathrm{raw}}S_{\theta}(x,y_{i}),\qquad A_{i}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathbb{I}\left\{R_{i}\geqslant\hat{r}_{m}\right\}\widetilde{R}_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(R_{i}), where η ^ m \hat{\eta}_{m} is computed from the same m m rollouts as in Eq. ( 10 ). In training, we use a practical stabilized version of the raw estimator: we take its positive part as a tail score and then center it within the prompt group A i TEA = ( A i raw ) + − 1 m ​ ∑ j = 1 m ( A j raw ) + . A_{i}^{\mathrm{TEA}}=\bigl(A_{i}^{\mathrm{raw}}\bigr)_{+}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigl(A_{j}^{\mathrm{raw}}\bigr)_{+}. Prefix-TEA denotes the advantage obtained from the fixed-order estimator in Theorem 2 . In the main experiments, we use the ( k , J ) = ( 2 , 4 ) (k,J)=(2,4) instance and apply the same positive-part and group-centering steps as in TEA. The implementation details are given in Appendix B.1 . Unless otherwise stated, both TEA and Prefix-TEA use α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 and N target = 128 N_{\mathrm{target}}=128 , which controls the tail-extrapolation curvature in the finite-rollout estimator.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare TEA and Prefix-TEA with GRPO and its normalized version GRPO-Z ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , as well as test-time-aware training baselines: BoN-max mean , BoN-max second , and BoN mean in ( Bagirov et al., 2025 ) , Chow BoN-RL in ( Chow et al., 2024 ) , and CAT-BoN , our implementation of the Best-of- N N rank-weighted scaling in ( Ousherovitch and Tewari, 2026 ) . All baselines are implemented as alternative advantage rules in the same grouped training interface. Our main comparisons use the matched per-prompt rollout budget m = 64 m=64 ; for test-time-aware baselines that naturally benefit from larger candidate sets, we also report m = 128 m=128 compute-unmatched tests. Full definitions, formulas, and compute-budget conventions are given in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: Main experimental setting.
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, our default setting trains meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on an UltraFeedback-derived instruction-following split ( Cui et al., 2023 ) , using Skywork/Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B as both the training reward model and the primary reward evaluator. We construct disjoint training, validation, and held-out evaluation prompt sets. For the comprehensive baseline comparison, we use core250 , a pre-specified 250-prompt held-out set on which we evaluate the full baseline suite. We additionally report results on core500 , a larger 500-prompt held-out set containing core250, for larger-scale confirmation of the key methods. The default training configuration uses rollout group size m = 64 m=64 , KL coefficient β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and 450 training steps. Checkpoints are selected using the same validation rule for all methods. Held-out evaluation samples 256 256 completions per prompt and reports grouped best-of- N N reward for N ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } N\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\} . For scaling experiments, we sample 512 512 completions per prompt to evaluate up to N = 512 N=512 . We report confidence intervals by paired prompt bootstrap. Full split construction, hyperparameters, validation protocol, and evaluation details are given in Appendix B.2 . Additional experiments vary the dataset, reward model, and policy backbone; each setting is introduced in the corresponding robustness subsection.

sections.heading: 4.3 Scaling with the train-time rollout budget

sections.text: Finally, we examine why TEA improves best-of- N N performance. Figure 3 (a) compares the actual gradients induced by different training methods with an empirical expected-best-of-128 oracle gradient. TEA is more aligned than GRPO and the strongest test-time-aware baseline across rollout budgets, supporting the claim that its finite-rollout advantage better approximates the desired best-of- N N update. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: We studied post-training for language models deployed with test-time strategies such as best-of- N N , where performance is governed by the upper tail of the reward distribution rather than the mean reward of a single response. To address the practical budget-mismatch regime m ≪ N m\ll N , we used test-time scaling-law structure to approximate the best-of- N N policy gradient from a small rollout group, leading to Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA) and its fixed-order debiased variant, Prefix-TEA. We provided finite-sample error and post-training guarantees, and showed empirically that these estimators improve best-of- N N performance over standard and test-time-aware baselines across datasets, reward models, and budget settings. This work also opens up a number of directions for future research. • We use a Gaussian upper-tail approximation to derive TEA and Prefix-TEA, but other tail structures could be used to construct different extrapolated estimators. In particular, it is interesting to explore methods that adapt to any tail structure, rather than relying on a fixed parametric form. Moreover, it is an important future direction to extend the idea to non-smooth reward distributions, such as zero-one rewards in the pass@ k k setting. • It is useful to extend the methods to other test-time strategies beyond best-of- N N , such as tree search methods, self-refine procedures, or interaction with external tools. In general, the tail-extrapolation principle applies to any test-time strategy that admits a scaling-law structure, but the specific form of the estimator and the training procedure may need to be adapted to the strategy and its scaling law.

sections.heading: Single-response post-training.
sections.text: Most LLM post-training methods are designed to improve the quality of a single sampled response. Reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) fine-tunes a policy against a learned reward model, typically with a KL penalty to keep the policy close to a reference model [ 13 ] . Preference-optimization methods such as DPO optimize an equivalent preference objective without explicitly running online RL [ 15 ] , while grouped policy-gradient methods such as GRPO improve the efficiency of RL-style post-training by normalizing rewards within a rollout group [ 19 ] . These methods are natural when the deployed model returns one response, but they do not directly optimize the multi-candidate behavior used by test-time strategies such as best-of- N N . This distinction is practically important because post-training changes not only the average quality of responses, but also the distribution of candidate responses at test time. Empirical studies show that RLHF, instruction tuning, and reward-based fine-tuning can reduce the diversity of generated candidates [ 9 , 14 ] . Complementary theory shows that reward variation also matters for optimization: if a reward model induces too little variance under the current policy, the RLHF objective can become flat and slow to optimize [ 16 ] . These works motivate a distributional view of post-training, but they do not specify how to optimize a target best-of- N N deployment objective.

sections.heading: Test-time strategies and test-time scaling.
sections.text: A separate line of work improves language model performance by spending more compute at deployment. Verifier-based methods generate many candidate solutions and return the one ranked highest by a verifier [ 6 ] . Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and aggregates their final answers [ 24 ] . Repeated-sampling studies show that coverage can increase predictably with the number of attempts, especially when candidate solutions can be automatically checked [ 4 ] . More broadly, test-time compute has become an independent scaling axis: it can be allocated to search, verifier scoring, adaptive procedures, or even problem-specific test-time training, and has been used to surpass prior human-engineered or best-known solutions in discovery-style tasks [ 20 , 25 , 11 ] . These results make the budget mismatch especially important. At deployment, one may spend a large amount of compute on a single hard prompt to find one exceptional response; during post-training, the same per-prompt budget is usually infeasible because optimization must cover many prompts. Best-of- N N is one of the simplest and most widely used instances of this principle. BoNBoN studies the best-of- N N distribution itself, relates it to KL-regularized alignment, and trains a model to mimic this distribution so that the sampling cost can be amortized [ 8 ] . Closest to our test-time scaling perspective, prior work shows that best-of- N N scaling laws can be predicted from m ≪ N m\ll N samples by extrapolating the upper tail of the reward distribution [ 10 ] . Our work uses the same high-level idea for a different purpose: rather than predicting the value of best-of- N N inference or amortizing its output distribution, we use tail extrapolation to construct a policy-gradient estimator for improving best-of- N N performance.

sections.heading: Test-time-aware post-training.
sections.text: Recent work directly adapts post-training to the deployment-time procedure. Best-of- N N -aware imitation-learning and RL objectives have been introduced [ 5 ] . Generic k k -sample test-time objectives, including pass@ k k and majority vote, have also been optimized [ 22 ] . Low-variance unbiased estimators have been derived for pass@ k k and its gradient [ 23 ] , and RL has been aligned with best-of- N N sampling through max@ k k optimization [ 1 ] . More general frameworks also show that alignment should depend on the test-time rule: InfAlign derives procedure-dependent reward transformations [ 3 ] , and Compute Aligned Training views test-time strategies as operators and derives corresponding training losses [ 12 ] . These works establish that post-training should account for how the model will be used at deployment. Our focus is the budget-mismatch regime left open by this line of work. Existing test-time-aware objectives typically construct their training signal by assuming access to the same per-prompt rollout budget as the deployment procedure. In contrast, we study the case where training observes only m ≪ N m\ll N rollouts per prompt, so the target best-of- N N objective cannot be directly formed during post-training. TEA uses the small training group only to estimate local upper-tail statistics, then extrapolates the corresponding gradient signal toward the larger best-of- N N deployment objective.

sections.heading: B.1 Estimator and Baseline Definitions
sections.text: We define all implemented training methods as alternative advantage rules A i A_{i} for the same prompt-level rollout group { ( y i , R i ) } i = 1 m \{(y_{i},R_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m} as in Section 4 . All advantages are treated as stop-gradient weights in the grouped training interface.

The direct plug-in estimator in ( 11 ) can be written in score-function form with raw advantage A i raw = 1 α 𝕀 { R i ⩾ r ^ m } R ~ η ^ m ( R i ) . sections.heading: Prefix-TEA (ours).
sections.text: Prefix-TEA is the implementation of the fixed-order estimator in Theorem 2 , with the specific form defined in ( 124 ). Let ( m 1 , … , m J ) (m_{1},\ldots,m_{J}) be the prescribed prefix sizes and ( w 1 , … , w J ) (w_{1},\ldots,w_{J}) the corresponding cancellation weights. For each prefix j j , we compute the empirical tail vector η ^ m j ( j ) \hat{\eta}_{m_{j}}^{(j)} using only the first m j m_{j} rewards in the rollout group, and define the prefix raw advantage A i , j raw = 𝕀 { i ⩽ m j } 1 α 𝕀 { R i ⩾ r ^ m j ( j ) } R ~ η ^ m j ( j ) ( R i ) . A_{i,j}^{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathbb{I}\left\{i\leqslant m_{j}\right\}\,\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathbb{I}\left\{R_{i}\geqslant\hat{r}_{m_{j}}^{(j)}\right\}\widetilde{R}_{\hat{\eta}_{m_{j}}^{(j)}}(R_{i}). (17) To express the weighted prefix gradients in the common full-group training interface, define ρ j := m / m j \rho_{j}:=m/m_{j} . We apply the same positive-part operation to each prefix raw advantage, combine the prefix scores with the fixed-order weights and the prefix-to-full-group scaling, and then center over the full rollout group: C i Prefix = ∑ j = 1 J w j ​ ρ j ​ ( A i , j raw ) + , A i Prefix ​ - ​ TEA = C i Prefix − 1 m ​ ∑ ℓ = 1 m C ℓ Prefix . C_{i}^{\mathrm{Prefix}}=\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_{j}\,\rho_{j}\,\bigl(A_{i,j}^{\mathrm{raw}}\bigr)_{+},\qquad A_{i}^{\mathrm{Prefix\text{-}TEA}}=C_{i}^{\mathrm{Prefix}}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}C_{\ell}^{\mathrm{Prefix}}. (18) In the main experiments we use the Prefix-TEA ( k , J ) = ( 2 , 4 ) (k,J)=(2,4) instance. For the default rollout group size m = 64 m=64 , this corresponds to prefix sizes ( m 1 , m 2 , m 3 , m 4 ) = ( 40 , 48 , 56 , 64 ) (m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4})=(40,48,56,64) and cancellation weights ( w 1 , w 2 , w 3 , w 4 ) = ( − 1.82946 , − 0.15392 , 1.04289 , 1.94050 ) . (w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4})=(-1.82946,\,-0.15392,\,1.04289,\,1.94050). The corresponding prefix-to-full-group scaling factors are ( ρ 1 , ρ 2 , ρ 3 , ρ 4 ) = ( 1.600 , 1.333 , 1.143 , 1.000 ) . (\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3},\rho_{4})=(1.600,\,1.333,\,1.143,\,1.000). The theoretical fixed-order estimator is stated in a cross-fitted form for analysis. Our main implementation uses fixed prefixes of the same rollout group, without a separate fit/evaluation split.

sections.heading: GRPO and GRPO-Z [ 19 ] .
sections.text: GRPO uses the mean-centered reward advantage A i GRPO = R i − R ¯ , R ¯ = 1 m ​ ∑ j = 1 m R j . A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=R_{i}-\bar{R},\qquad\bar{R}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_{j}. (19) GRPO-Z is the group-normalized variant, A i GRPO ​ - ​ Z = R i − R ¯ std ⁡ ( R 1 , … , R m ) + ε . A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO\text{-}Z}}=\frac{R_{i}-\bar{R}}{\operatorname{std}(R_{1},\ldots,R_{m})+\varepsilon}. (20) We use GRPO-Z as an advantage-scale control.

sections.heading: BoN-max mean and BoN-max second [ 1 ] .
sections.text: These are selected-output BoN baselines following the BoN-max baselines listed in [ 1 ] . Let i ⋆ = arg ⁡ max i ⁡ R i , R ⋆ = R i ⋆ , i^{\star}=\arg\max_{i}R_{i},\qquad R^{\star}=R_{i^{\star}}, with deterministic tie-breaking, and let R ( 2 ) R^{(2)} denote the second-largest reward in the group. BoN-max mean gives nonzero advantage only to the reward-selected response: A i BoN ​ - ​ max ​ mean = { R ⋆ − R ¯ , i = i ⋆ , 0 , otherwise . A_{i}^{\mathrm{BoN\text{-}max\ mean}}=\begin{cases}R^{\star}-\bar{R},&i=i^{\star},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (21) BoN-max second instead uses the runner-up reward as the baseline: A i BoN ​ - ​ max ​ second = { R ⋆ − R ( 2 ) , i = i ⋆ , 0 , otherwise . A_{i}^{\mathrm{BoN\text{-}max\ second}}=\begin{cases}R^{\star}-R^{(2)},&i=i^{\star},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (22)

sections.heading: BoN mean [ 1 ] .
sections.text: We use the name BoN mean for the transformed-reward baseline derived from the max@ k k objective in [ 1 ] . Let the rewards be sorted in ascending order, r ( 1 ) ⩽ r ( 2 ) ⩽ ⋯ ⩽ r ( m ) . r_{(1)}\leqslant r_{(2)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant r_{(m)}. For a target subset size k < m k<m , define the transformed reward at sorted position i i as B ( i ) = r ( i ) ​ ( i − 1 k − 1 ) ( m k ) + ∑ j > i r ( j ) ​ ( j − 2 k − 2 ) ( m k ) . B_{(i)}=r_{(i)}\frac{\binom{i-1}{k-1}}{\binom{m}{k}}+\sum_{j>i}r_{(j)}\frac{\binom{j-2}{k-2}}{\binom{m}{k}}. (23) We unsort B ( i ) B_{(i)} back to the original sample order and use the group-normalized advantage A i Max ​ @ ​ K = B i − B ¯ std ⁡ ( B 1 , … , B m ) + ε . A_{i}^{\mathrm{Max@K}}=\frac{B_{i}-\bar{B}}{\operatorname{std}(B_{1},\ldots,B_{m})+\varepsilon}. (24) The exact Max@ k k transformation requires k < m k<m . In the matched m = 64 m=64 setting we use k = 32 k=32 ; in the m = 128 m=128 stress tests we use k = 64 k=64 .

sections.heading: Chow BoN-RL [ 5 ] .
sections.text: We implement a Monte Carlo estimator of the Lemma 2 BoN-RL gradient in [ 5 ] , under the scalar reward-model specialization R = r R=r and prompt baseline b = 0 b=0 . For a group of size m m , we randomly split the group into a BoN selection set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} of size N sel N_{\mathrm{sel}} and an independent correction set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} of size M corr M_{\mathrm{corr}} , with N sel + M corr = m N_{\mathrm{sel}}+M_{\mathrm{corr}}=m . Let i ⋆ = arg ⁡ max i ∈ 𝒮 ⁡ R i , R ⋆ = R i ⋆ . i^{\star}=\arg\max_{i\in\mathcal{S}}R_{i},\qquad R^{\star}=R_{i^{\star}}. The selected BoN response receives the selected-response term, and correction samples receive the Lemma 2 correction term: A i Chow = m [ 𝕀 { i = i ⋆ } R ⋆ − 𝕀 { i ∈ 𝒞 } λ N sel M corr 𝕀 { R i > R ⋆ } R ⋆ ] . A_{i}^{\mathrm{Chow}}=m\left[\mathbb{I}\left\{i=i^{\star}\right\}R^{\star}-\mathbb{I}\left\{i\in\mathcal{C}\right\}\,\frac{\lambda_{N_{\mathrm{sel}}}}{M_{\mathrm{corr}}}\mathbb{I}\left\{R_{i}>R^{\star}\right\}\,R^{\star}\right]. (25) Here λ N sel \lambda_{N_{\mathrm{sel}}} is the coefficient appearing in Chow et al.’s Lemma 2 for a BoN selection set of size N sel N_{\mathrm{sel}} . The prefactor m m accounts for the fact that our trainer averages the loss over the m m sampled responses. In the matched m = 64 m=64 setting we use N sel = 32 N_{\mathrm{sel}}=32 and M corr = 32 M_{\mathrm{corr}}=32 ; in the m = 128 m=128 stress tests we use a 64 / 64 64/64 split. We should note that in [ 5 ] , the authors target verifier-selected BoN inference and report pass@ K K evaluations, whereas our setting uses a learned reward model for instruction-following. We therefore compare the Lemma 2 estimator under a matched rollout budget rather than reproducing their full experimental setup.

sections.heading: CAT-BoN [ 12 ] .
sections.text: CAT-BoN follows the Compute Aligned Training principle in [ 12 ] , which reweights gradients by the marginal utility of a sample under a test-time strategy. For BoN, we use a rank-based scaling. Let F ^ < ​ ( R i ) \hat{F}_{<}(R_{i}) be the empirical fraction of group rewards strictly below R i R_{i} , with the same tie-handling rule used in the implementation. We define w i = N target ​ F ^ < ​ ( R i ) N target − 1 , w ~ i = w i 1 m ​ ∑ j = 1 m w j + ε . w_{i}=N_{\mathrm{target}}\,\hat{F}_{<}(R_{i})^{N_{\mathrm{target}}-1},\qquad\tilde{w}_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{j}+\varepsilon}. (26) CAT-BoN applies this normalized rank weight to the group-normalized reward advantage: A i CAT = w ~ i ​ R i − R ¯ std ⁡ ( R 1 , … , R m ) + ε . A_{i}^{\mathrm{CAT}}=\tilde{w}_{i}\,\frac{R_{i}-\bar{R}}{\operatorname{std}(R_{1},\ldots,R_{m})+\varepsilon}. (27) Unless otherwise stated, we use N target = 128 N_{\mathrm{target}}=128 for CAT-BoN.

sections.heading: UltraFeedback splits.
sections.text: We construct fixed, disjoint training, validation, and held-out evaluation prompt sets from UltraFeedback [ 7 ] . After deduplication and removing prompts overlapping the source test split, the eligible pool contains 37,756 prompts. We use 34,994 prompts for policy training, 512 prompts as a validation pool, and 2,000 prompts as a held-out final pool. The main comprehensive baseline comparison uses core250 , a deterministic 250-prompt held-out subset. We also use core500 , a larger 500-prompt held-out set containing core250, to confirm the main method ordering on a larger evaluation set. Training, validation, and held-out evaluation prompts are disjoint.

sections.heading: Checkpoint selection.
sections.text: All methods use the same checkpoint-selection rule. Each 25 25 training steps, we evaluate the current checkpoint on the validation pool. Specifically, for each checkpoint, we sample 32 completions for each of 128 fixed validation prompts and score them with the reward model. We compute the mean reward of the top 10 completions for each prompt, average this value over prompts, and select the checkpoint with the highest average. Validation prompts are used only for checkpoint selection and are never used for held-out reporting.

sections.heading: Reported best-of- N N reward scores.
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, all reported bo N N values are reward-model scores under the grouped best-of- N N evaluation protocol. For each held-out prompt x x , we sample M M completions and score them as R i = R ⁡ ( x , y i ) R_{i}=R(x,y_{i}) . For a reported budget N N dividing M M , we partition the M M completions into M / N M/N consecutive groups of size N N , take the maximum reward in each group, average these maxima within the prompt, and then average over prompts. For the main held-out evaluation, M = 256 M=256 and N ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } N\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\} . The m m -to- N N scaling experiments use M = 512 M=512 and report bo128, bo256, and bo512.

sections.heading: Uncertainty estimates.
sections.text: Confidence intervals are computed using paired prompt bootstrap with 1,000 resamples. Prompt-level win/tie/loss is computed from the same prompt-level grouped best-of- k k values: a method wins a prompt if its value is larger than the comparison method, loses if it is smaller, and ties if the absolute difference is at most 10 − 9 10^{-9} . What’s more, all reported experiments were run on NVIDIA L40S GPU workers with 48GB GPU memory per device.

The unweighted local L 2 L^{2} and L 1 L^{1} bounds follow from the weighted bounds because the weights are at least one on ℰ 1 \mathcal{E}_{1} . It remains only to control the complement ℰ 1 c \mathcal{E}_{1}^{c} . By Cauchy–Schwarz, the empirical tail moment envelope in Lemma 5 , and ℙ ⁡ ( ℰ 1 c ) ⩽ C ​ e − c ​ m \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{1}^{c})\leqslant Ce^{-cm} , 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ 2 ​ 𝕀 ​ { ℰ 1 c } ] ⩽ C ​ e − c ​ m . \mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|^{2}\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{1}^{c}\right\}\right]\leqslant Ce^{-cm}. Therefore, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C m 2 . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant\frac{C}{m^{2}}. The L 1 L^{1} bound follows by Cauchy–Schwarz: 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ ] ⩽ ( 𝔼 ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ 2 ) 1 / 2 ⩽ C m . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|\bigr]\leqslant\left(\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leqslant\frac{C}{m}. This completes the proof. ∎ The next lemma isolates the same-batch error of the direct plug-in estimator. Although η ^ m \hat{\eta}_{m} is computed from the same samples used in P m P_{m} , the plug-in fluctuation remains O ⁡ ( log ⁡ N / m ) O(\log N/m) in second moment, and the resulting empirical-process bias is only O ⁡ ( log ⁡ N / m ) O(\sqrt{\log N}/m) . Lemma 11 . Under Assumptions 1 , 2 , and 3 , for all sufficiently large m m , 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ P m ​ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m , \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl\|P_{m}(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta})\bigr\|^{2}\Bigr]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}, (101) and ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \left\|\mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]\right\|\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. (102) Proof. The main issue is that η ^ m \hat{\eta}_{m} is computed from the same batch used in P m P_{m} , so η ^ m \hat{\eta}_{m} is not independent of the summands. We remove this dependence by inserting the leave-one-out vector η ^ m ( − i ) \hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-i)} , which is independent of y i y_{i} , and then control the leave-one-out perturbation. We first prove ( 101 ). By Jensen’s inequality, ‖ P m ​ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ) ‖ 2 ⩽ P m ​ ‖ φ η ^ m − φ η ‖ 2 . \bigl\|P_{m}(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta})\bigr\|^{2}\leqslant P_{m}\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}. By exchangeability, it is enough to control the expectation of the first summand. Decompose φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ​ ( y 1 ) = ( φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ​ ( y 1 ) ) + ( φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) ) . \varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{1})=\bigl(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{1})\bigr)+\bigl(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})\bigr). For the first term, η ^ m ( − 1 ) \hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)} is independent of y 1 y_{1} . Therefore, using Lemma 7 and Corollary 2 for sample size m − 1 m-1 , 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ​ ( y 1 ) ‖ 2 ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{1})\|^{2}\bigr] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ P ​ ‖ φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) − φ η ‖ 2 ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}-\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}\Big] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ 𝔼 ​ ‖ η ^ m ( − 1 ) − η ‖ 2 + C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m \displaystyle\leqslant C\log N\,\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}-\eta\|^{2}+C\log N\,e^{-cm} ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \displaystyle\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}. Here and below, bad events are events on which an empirical tail vector leaves B ⁡ ( η , δ reg ) B(\eta,\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}) . On such events we use the following crude bound. By the definition of φ η ′ \varphi_{\eta^{\prime}} in ( 38 ), ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y ) ‖ 2 ⩽ G 2 α 2 ​ | R ~ η ^ m ​ ( R ⁡ ( y ) ) | 2 , \|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y)\|^{2}\leqslant\frac{G^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}\left|\widetilde{R}_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(R(y))\right|^{2}, where we used Assumption 2 . By the explicit form of the shaped reward, R ~ η ^ m ​ ( u ) = ( u − r ^ m ) + c ~ N 2 ​ σ ^ m ​ ( ( u − μ ^ m ) 2 − ( r ^ m − μ ^ m ) 2 ) . \widetilde{R}_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(u)=(u-\hat{r}_{m})+\frac{\widetilde{c}_{N}}{2\hat{\sigma}_{m}}\left((u-\hat{\mu}_{m})^{2}-(\hat{r}_{m}-\hat{\mu}_{m})^{2}\right). Using ( 42 ) and the clipping σ ^ m ⩾ ε σ \hat{\sigma}_{m}\geqslant\varepsilon_{\sigma} , we obtain | R ~ η ^ m ​ ( u ) | ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ ( 1 + | u | 2 + | r ^ m | 2 + | μ ^ m | 2 ) . \left|\widetilde{R}_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(u)\right|\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\left(1+|u|^{2}+|\hat{r}_{m}|^{2}+|\hat{\mu}_{m}|^{2}\right). Consequently, ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y ) ‖ 2 ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ⁡ ( 1 + | R ⁡ ( y ) | 4 + | r ^ m | 4 + | μ ^ m | 4 ) . \|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y)\|^{2}\leqslant C\log N\left(1+|R(y)|^{4}+|\hat{r}_{m}|^{4}+|\hat{\mu}_{m}|^{4}\right). (103) The empirical terms in this bound are controlled by the moment envelope in Lemma 5 , while the R ⁡ ( y ) R(y) term is controlled by Assumption 1 , namely 𝔼 ⁡ [ R 4 ] ⩽ M R \mathbb{E}[R^{4}]\leqslant M_{R} . Combining ( 103 ) with the exponential localization probability gives a C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m C\log Ne^{-cm} contribution in squared bounds and a C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m C\sqrt{\log N}e^{-cm} contribution in first-moment bounds. For the second term, the pointwise local bound ( 77 ) and the weighted leave-one-out bound ( 96 ) give 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) ‖ 2 ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})\|^{2}\bigr] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ( 1 + | R 1 | 4 ) ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ 2 ​ 𝕀 ​ { η ^ m , η ^ m ( − 1 ) ∈ B ⁡ ( η , δ reg ) } ] + C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m \displaystyle\leqslant C\log N\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(1+|R_{1}|^{4})\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|^{2}\mathbb{I}\left\{\hat{\eta}_{m},\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\in B(\eta,\delta_{\mathrm{reg}})\right\}\right]+C\log N\,e^{-cm} ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m 2 + C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m . \displaystyle\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m^{2}}+C\log N\,e^{-cm}. Combining the two terms gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ​ ( y 1 ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{1})\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}. And thus: 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ P m ​ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ 1 m ​ ∑ i = 1 m 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y i ) − φ η ​ ( y i ) ‖ 2 ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ​ ( y 1 ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m , \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl\|P_{m}(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta})\bigr\|^{2}\Bigr]\leqslant\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{i})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{i})\|^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\eta}(y_{1})\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}, which proves ( 101 ). We now prove the same-batch bias bound ( 102 ). By exchangeability, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − P ​ φ η ^ m ] . \mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-P\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]. Insert the leave-one-out vector η ^ m ( − 1 ) \hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)} . Since η ^ m ( − 1 ) \hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)} is independent of y 1 y_{1} , 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) − P ​ φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ] = 0 . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})-P\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}\bigr]=0. Therefore, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})\bigr] − 𝔼 ⁡ [ P ⁡ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ) ] . \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\bigl[P(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}})\bigr]. For the first term, the pointwise local bound and ( 97 ) give 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ φ η ^ m ​ ( y 1 ) − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ​ ( y 1 ) ‖ ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}(y_{1})-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}(y_{1})\|\bigr] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ( 1 + | R 1 | 2 ) ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ ​ 𝕀 ​ { η ^ m , η ^ m ( − 1 ) ∈ B ⁡ ( η , δ reg ) } ] + C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m \displaystyle\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(1+|R_{1}|^{2})\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|\mathbb{I}\left\{\hat{\eta}_{m},\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\in B(\eta,\delta_{\mathrm{reg}})\right\}\right]+C\sqrt{\log N}\,e^{-cm} ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \displaystyle\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. For the second term, Jensen’s inequality and Lemma 7 imply 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ P ⁡ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ) ‖ ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|P(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}})\|\bigr] ⩽ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P ​ ‖ φ η ^ m − φ η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ 2 ) 1 / 2 ] \displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{E}\Big[\bigl(P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}}\|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}\Big] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ 𝔼 ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ^ m ( − 1 ) ‖ + C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m \displaystyle\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\,\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\hat{\eta}_{m}^{(-1)}\|+C\sqrt{\log N}\,e^{-cm} ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \displaystyle\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. Combining the two bounds proves ( 102 ). ∎ We’re now ready to prove the main result on the direct plug-in estimator. Proof of Theorem 1 . Fix x x and θ \theta . Throughout the proof, write g ^ m dir ​ ( θ , x ) = P m ​ φ η ^ m , g θ ​ ( x ) = P ​ φ η . \widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}(\theta;x)=P_{m}\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}},\qquad g_{\theta}(x)=P\varphi_{\eta}.

sections.heading: Variance.
sections.text: Since variance is minimized by centering at the mean, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ g ^ m dir − 𝔼 ⁡ [ g ^ m dir ] ‖ 2 ] ⩽ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ g ^ m dir − g θ ​ ( x ) ‖ 2 ] . \mathbb{E}\Big[\bigl\|\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}]\bigr\|^{2}\Big]\leqslant\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}-g_{\theta}(x)\|^{2}\bigr]. Decompose g ^ m dir − g θ ​ ( x ) = ( P m ​ φ η − P ​ φ η ) + P m ​ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ) . \widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}-g_{\theta}(x)=(P_{m}\varphi_{\eta}-P\varphi_{\eta})+P_{m}(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta}). The first term comes from the Monte Carlo fluctuation of the ideal estimator P m ​ φ η P_{m}\varphi_{\eta} , and we have: 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ P m ​ φ η − P ​ φ η ‖ 2 ] ⩽ 1 m ​ P ​ ‖ φ η ‖ 2 ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m , \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|P_{m}\varphi_{\eta}-P\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant\frac{1}{m}P\|\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}, where we used Lemma 7 . The plug-in term is controlled by Lemma 11 : 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ P m ​ ( φ η ^ m − φ η ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\bigl\|P_{m}(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-\varphi_{\eta})\bigr\|^{2}\Bigr]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}. Therefore, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ g ^ m dir − 𝔼 ⁡ [ g ^ m dir ] ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \mathbb{E}\Big[\bigl\|\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}]\bigr\|^{2}\Big]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{m}.

sections.heading: Bias.
sections.text: We decompose the bias as 𝔼 ⁡ [ g ^ m dir ] − g θ ​ ( x ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] + 𝔼 ⁡ [ P ​ φ η ^ m − P ​ φ η ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] + 𝔼 ⁡ [ H ⁡ ( η ^ m ) − H ⁡ ( η ) ] . \mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}]-g_{\theta}(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[P\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}-P\varphi_{\eta}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[H(\hat{\eta}_{m})-H(\eta)\bigr]. The first term comes from evaluating the plug-in estimator on the same batch used to compute η ^ m \hat{\eta}_{m} , and is bounded by Lemma 11 : ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( P m − P ) ​ φ η ^ m ] ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \left\|\mathbb{E}\bigl[(P_{m}-P)\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{m}}\bigr]\right\|\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. It remains to control the population plug-in term. Let ℰ m := { η ^ m ∈ B ( η , δ reg ) } . \mathcal{E}_{m}:=\{\hat{\eta}_{m}\in B(\eta,\delta_{\mathrm{reg}})\}. where δ reg \delta_{\mathrm{reg}} is as in Lemma 7 . On ℰ m \mathcal{E}_{m} , Lemma 7 gives H ⁡ ( η ^ m ) − H ⁡ ( η ) = H ˙ η ​ ( η ^ m − η ) + ℛ m , ‖ ℛ m ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ‖ 2 . H(\hat{\eta}_{m})-H(\eta)=\dot{H}_{\eta}(\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta)+\mathcal{R}_{m},\qquad\|\mathcal{R}_{m}\|\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\,\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta\|^{2}. Therefore, 𝔼 ⁡ [ H ⁡ ( η ^ m ) − H ⁡ ( η ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[H(\hat{\eta}_{m})-H(\eta)] = H ˙ η ​ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ η ^ m ] − η ) + 𝔼 ⁡ [ ℛ m ​ 𝕀 ​ { ℰ m } ] \displaystyle=\dot{H}_{\eta}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\eta}_{m}]-\eta\bigr)+\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}_{m}\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{m}\right\}] − H ˙ η ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ( η ^ m − η ) ​ 𝕀 ​ { ℰ m c } ] + 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( H ⁡ ( η ^ m ) − H ⁡ ( η ) ) ​ 𝕀 ​ { ℰ m c } ] . \displaystyle-\dot{H}_{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}[(\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta)\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{m}^{c}\right\}]+\mathbb{E}[(H(\hat{\eta}_{m})-H(\eta))\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{m}^{c}\right\}]. The first term is bounded by ‖ H ˙ η ‖ ​ ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ η ^ m ] − η ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ⋅ 1 m . \|\dot{H}_{\eta}\|\,\|\mathbb{E}[\hat{\eta}_{m}]-\eta\|\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\cdot\frac{1}{m}. where we used Lemma 7 and the bias bound in Corollary 2 . For the remainder term on the good event, by the second-moment bound in Corollary 2 and 𝕀 ​ { ℰ m } ⩽ 1 \mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{m}\right\}\leqslant 1 , 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ ℛ m ‖ ​ 𝕀 ​ { ℰ m } ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ​ 𝔼 ​ ‖ η ^ m − η ‖ 2 ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{R}_{m}\|\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{m}\right\}]\leqslant C\sqrt{\log N}\,\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta\|^{2}\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. For the two complement terms, ℙ ⁡ ( ℰ m c ) ⩽ C ​ e − c ​ m \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{m}^{c})\leqslant Ce^{-cm} by Corollary 2 . Using the empirical tail moment envelope and the polynomial growth of H ⁡ ( η ′ ) = P ​ φ η ′ H(\eta^{\prime})=P\varphi_{\eta^{\prime}} , their total contribution is C ​ log ⁡ N ​ e − c ​ m , C\sqrt{\log N}\,e^{-cm}, which is absorbed into C ​ log ⁡ N / m C\sqrt{\log N}/m for sufficiently large m m . Hence ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ H ⁡ ( η ^ m ) − H ⁡ ( η ) ] ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \left\|\mathbb{E}[H(\hat{\eta}_{m})-H(\eta)]\right\|\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. Combining this with the same-batch bias bound yields ‖ 𝔼 ⁡ [ g ^ m dir ​ ( θ , x ) ] − g θ ​ ( x ) ‖ ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N m . \bigl\|\mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}_{m}^{\mathrm{dir}}(\theta;x)]-g_{\theta}(x)\bigr\|\leqslant C\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{m}. This proves ( 12 ). ∎

sections.heading: Cross-fitted base estimator.
sections.text: We first record the basic properties of the cross-fitted plug-in gradient. We state the result for a generic base sample size n n , since the fixed-order estimator will later combine estimators evaluated at prefix sizes n 1 , … , n J n_{1},\dots,n_{J} . For such an n n , draw two independent batches 𝒟 A = { y i ( A ) } i = 1 n , 𝒟 B = { y i ( B ) } i = 1 n , \mathcal{D}_{A}=\{y_{i}^{(A)}\}_{i=1}^{n},\qquad\mathcal{D}_{B}=\{y_{i}^{(B)}\}_{i=1}^{n}, with all samples drawn i.i.d. from π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) . Let η ^ n ( A ) = ( r ^ n ( A ) , μ ^ n ( A ) , σ ^ n ( A ) ) \hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}=(\hat{r}_{n}^{(A)},\hat{\mu}_{n}^{(A)},\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{(A)}) be the empirical tail vector computed from batch A A in the same way as ( 10 ). Define P n ( B ) ​ f := 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n f ⁡ ( y i ( B ) ) . P_{n}^{(B)}f:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(y_{i}^{(B)}). Then the cross-fitted base estimator can be written as G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) := P n ( B ) ​ φ η ^ n ( A ) . G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x):=P_{n}^{(B)}\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}. (104) Lemma 12 . Suppose Assumptions 1 , 2 , and 3 hold. Then, 𝔼 ⁡ [ G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ H ⁡ ( η ^ n ) ] , \mathbb{E}\!\left[G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x)\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[H(\hat{\eta}_{n})\right], (105) where η ^ n \hat{\eta}_{n} denotes an empirical tail vector computed from an independent size- n n batch. Moreover, for all sufficiently large n n , 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) − 𝔼 ⁡ [ G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) ] ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N n . \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x)-\mathbb{E}[G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x)]\right\|^{2}\right]\leqslant C\frac{\log N}{n}. (106) The constant C C depends only on ( α , G , σ min , M R ) (\alpha,G,\sigma_{\min},M_{R}) . Proof. Let ℱ A := σ ⁡ ( 𝒟 A ) \mathcal{F}_{A}:=\sigma(\mathcal{D}_{A}) be the sigma-field generated by the tail-estimation batch. Conditional on ℱ A \mathcal{F}_{A} , the vector η ^ n ( A ) \hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)} is fixed and the evaluation samples in batch B B are i.i.d. Therefore, 𝔼 ⁡ [ G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) | ℱ A ] = P ​ φ η ^ n ( A ) = H ⁡ ( η ^ n ( A ) ) . \mathbb{E}\!\left[G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x)\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right]=P\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}=H(\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}). Taking expectations gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ G n cf ​ ( θ , x ) ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ H ⁡ ( η ^ n ( A ) ) ] . \mathbb{E}[G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}(\theta;x)]=\mathbb{E}[H(\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)})]. Since η ^ n ( A ) \hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)} has the same distribution as an independent size- n n empirical tail vector η ^ n \hat{\eta}_{n} , this proves ( 105 ). It remains to prove the variance bound. Write H A := H ⁡ ( η ^ n ( A ) ) . H_{A}:=H(\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}). We decompose G n cf − 𝔼 ⁡ [ G n cf ] = ( G n cf − H A ) + ( H A − 𝔼 ​ H A ) . G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-\mathbb{E}[G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}]=\bigl(G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-H_{A}\bigr)+\bigl(H_{A}-\mathbb{E}H_{A}\bigr). Thus 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ G n cf − 𝔼 ​ G n cf ‖ 2 ] ⩽ 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ‖ G n cf − H A ‖ 2 ] + 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ‖ H A − 𝔼 ​ H A ‖ 2 ] . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-\mathbb{E}G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant 2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-H_{A}\|^{2}\bigr]+2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|H_{A}-\mathbb{E}H_{A}\|^{2}\bigr]. (107) The first term captures the noise of evaluating the plug-in estimator on batch B B . Conditional on ℱ A \mathcal{F}_{A} , G n cf − H A = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n ( φ η ^ n ( A ) ​ ( y i ( B ) ) − P ​ φ η ^ n ( A ) ) , G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-H_{A}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}(y_{i}^{(B)})-P\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}\right), where the summands are i.i.d. and mean zero. Hence 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ G n cf − H A ‖ 2 | ℱ A ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G_{n}^{\mathrm{cf}}-H_{A}\|^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right] ⩽ 1 n ​ P ​ ‖ φ η ^ n ( A ) ‖ 2 . \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n}P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}\|^{2}. (108) We claim that 𝔼 ⁡ [ P ​ ‖ φ η ^ n ( A ) ‖ 2 ] ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N . \mathbb{E}\!\left[P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}\|^{2}\right]\leqslant C\log N. (109) Indeed, on the event η ^ n ( A ) ∈ B ⁡ ( η , δ reg ) \hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}\in B(\eta,\delta_{\mathrm{reg}}) , by Lemma 7 , P ​ ‖ φ η ^ n ( A ) ‖ 2 ⩽ 2 ​ P ​ ‖ φ η ‖ 2 + 2 ​ P ​ ‖ φ η ^ n ( A ) − φ η ‖ 2 ⩽ C ​ log ⁡ N ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ η ^ n ( A ) − η ‖ 2 ) . P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}\|^{2}\leqslant 2P\|\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}+2P\|\varphi_{\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}}-\varphi_{\eta}\|^{2}\leqslant C\log N\bigl(1+\|\hat{\eta}_{n}^{(A)}-\eta\|^{2}\bigr). sections.heading: Purpose.
sections.text: This section is a diagnostic for the fixed-order debiasing theorem. It is not a training benchmark. We isolate the finite-sample bias–variance tradeoff in a one-prompt Gaussian-tail model where the target gradient is known analytically. The goal is to check that Prefix-TEA cancels systematic bias, while also giving guidance on the budget regimes where prefix-TEA is expected to outperform TEA.

sections.heading: Synthetic model.
sections.text: We take R = Z , Z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) , R=Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), with bounded two-dimensional score S ( Z ) = ( 𝕀 { Z ⩾ 1.0 } − Φ ¯ ( 1.0 ) , 𝕀 { Z ⩾ 1.5 } − Φ ¯ ( 1.5 ) ) . S(Z)=\bigl(\mathbb{I}\left\{Z\geqslant 1.0\right\}-\bar{\Phi}(1.0),\mathbb{I}\left\{Z\geqslant 1.5\right\}-\bar{\Phi}(1.5)\bigr). We set α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 and N = 128 N=128 . The true gradient is computed from exact Gaussian tail integrals. We compare prefix-TEA to TEA with the same rollout budget m m and prompt batch size P P .

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: For a prompt batch of size P P , we report MSE P ⁡ ( m ) = ‖ Bias ⁡ ( m ) ‖ 2 2 + Var ⁡ ( m ) P . \operatorname{MSE}_{P}(m)=\|\operatorname{Bias}(m)\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(m)}{P}. For Prefix-TEA, systematic bias is estimated by Rao–Blackwellizing over the evaluation split; variance is measured using the actual finite-sample estimator. We report the main Prefix-TEA setting k = 2 , J = 4 k=2,J=4 , and include J = 8 J=8 as a stabilizing ablation.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 4 gives the bias and variance scaling with m m for P = 1 P=1 . The bias plot confirms second-order cancellation for the main k = 2 , J = 4 k=2,J=4 Prefix-TEA diagnostic: its bias decreases faster than TEA and follows the expected m − 2 m^{-2} trend in the large- m m regime. The variance plot shows the cost: Prefix-TEA has a larger variance constant. Figure 5 then shows how this bias–variance tradeoff changes after prompt-batch averaging. For small P P , the larger Prefix-TEA variance dominates, so TEA has lower MSE. As P P increases, the variance term is suppressed and the smaller Prefix-TEA bias becomes decisive, producing the blue region where Prefix-TEA outperforms TEA. Table 15 quantifies the same effect: Prefix-TEA has worse one-prompt MSE, but crosses over once P P reaches the thousands range, depending on m m and J J . Figure 4 : Bias and variance scaling in the one-prompt Gaussian-tail diagnostic. Prefix-TEA k = 2 , J = 4 k=2,J=4 reduces systematic bias faster than TEA, but with a larger variance constant. Figure 5 : Prompt-batch frontier for Prefix-TEA k = 2 , J = 4 k=2,J=4 , with J = 8 J=8 as a stabilizing ablation. sections.heading: Takeaway.
sections.text: The diagnostic explains why Prefix-TEA can underperform TEA in small-budget real training runs despite its higher-order bias cancellation: the variance and constant factors matter. Its advantage appears in the large-rollout and large-prompt-batch regime where the reduced bias floor dominates.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2605.10716v1 [cs.LG] 11 May 2026 What should post-training optimize? A test-time scaling law perspective Muheng Li † Jian Qian ⋄ Wenlong Mou † Department of Statistical Sciences, University of Toronto † Department of AI and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong ⋄ Abstract Large language models are increasingly deployed with test-time strategies: sample N N responses, score them with a reward model or verifier, and return the best. This deployment rule exposes a mismatch in post-training: standard objectives optimize the mean reward of a single response, whereas best-of- N N performance is governed by the upper tail of the reward distribution. Recent test-time-aware objectives partly address this mismatch, but typically assume that training can use the same per-prompt rollout budget as deployment, which is impractical when post-training must cover many prompts while deployment can allocate much larger per-prompt test-time compute. We study this budget-mismatch regime, where only m ≪ N m\ll N per-prompt rollouts are available during training but the target objective is best-of- N N deployment. Under structural assumptions on the reward tails, we show that the policy gradient of the best-of- N N objective can be approximated from a much smaller rollout group by extrapolating upper-tail statistics. This yields a family of Tail-Extrapolated estimators for best-of- N N -oriented post-training: a simple direct estimator, Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA), and a fixed-order debiased Prefix-TEA estimator based on moment cancellation. Experiments on instruction-following tasks show that TEA and Prefix-TEA improve best-of- N N performance across different language models, reward models and datasets under various training and test-time budget settings. 1 Introduction The modern workflow for large language models (LLM) typically consists of three stages: pre-training, post-training, and test-time adaptation. Post-training is a critical stage in the development of large language models (LLMs), where a pre-trained model is further fine-tuned using reinforcement learning to optimize a task-specific objective or align with human preferences. At deployment time, practitioners often use additional test-time compute to improve performance. A widely used strategy is best-of- N N sampling: for each prompt, one draws N N independent responses from the model, scores them with a reward model, and returns the one with the largest score. This test-time strategy can substantially improve performance, but it also creates a mismatch with the standard post-training objective, which optimizes the expected reward of a single response rather than the best response among N N samples. This mismatch is not only conceptually unsatisfying, but also practically sub-optimal. Empirically, reward-guided fine-tuning has been shown to reduce output diversity across different tasks, which removes precisely the stochasticity that the best-of- N N (BoN) sampling strategy relies on ( Kirk et al., 2023 ; O’Mahony et al., 2024 ) . Direct test-time-aware training studies give complementary evidence: BoN-aware, pass@ k k /majority-vote-aware, and max@ k k objectives improve best-of- N N or set-level performance on various benchmarks over standard single-sample objectives ( Chow et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Bagirov et al., 2025 ; Ousherovitch and Tewari, 2026 ) . These test-time-aware post-training methods typically involve computing the test-time objective directly during training, which requires a large rollout budget per prompt. For example, if the test-time strategy is best-of- N N sampling, then for each prompt during training, one needs to generate at least N N responses to compute the objective and the policy gradient. This matched-budget requirement creates tension between post-training and test-time deployment. On the one hand, post-training must cover a large number of prompts, so the rollout budget available for each individual prompt is often limited ( Zhang and Zuo, 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . On the other hand, test-time compute is increasingly treated as a separate scaling dimension, and recent work has begun to study deployment regimes with substantially larger search budgets ( Snell et al., 2024 ; Chow et al., 2024 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ) . This motivates the key question: Can we optimize best-of- N N performance when only m ≪ N m\ll N rollouts per prompt are available during training? In this paper, we provide a solution to this question through the lens of test-time scaling laws , which characterize how best-of- N N performance scales with N N under a given policy. Recently, Li et al., Li et al. (2026) characterize the BoN scaling law by modeling the upper tail of the reward distribution, and show that the BoN scaling law can be predicted using m ≪ N m\ll N samples by extrapolating upper-tail statistics. Drawing on this perspective, we develop a family of algorithms that use tail extrapolation to optimize best-of- N N performance under a small rollout budget. Our main contributions are as follows: • We derive a class of Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA) estimators for the advantage function and policy gradient of the best-of- N N objective, which can be estimated from m ≪ N m\ll N rollouts per prompt. We further construct a debiased estimator, Prefix-TEA, which further removes the bias in stochastic gradient estimation. • We prove non-asymptotic gradient estimation error bounds for TEA and Prefix-TEA, characterizing the bias–variance tradeoff and the dependence on the training budget m m and the test-time budget N N . Building upon these guarantees, we establish convergence guarantees for post-training with TEA and Prefix-TEA, with respect to the best-of- N N objective. • We conduct extensive experiments on instruction-following tasks, showing that TEA and Prefix-TEA consistently improve best-of- N N performance over GRPO and recent test-time-aware baselines across datasets and reward models under various training and test-time budget settings. We provide a detailed discussion of related work in Appendix A . 2 Problem setup and test-time-aware objective 2.1 Text generation and reward distribution Let x ∼ P X x\sim P_{X} be a prompt. Baselines. All baselines are implemented as alternative advantage rules in the same grouped training interface. Our main comparisons use the matched per-prompt rollout budget m = 64 m=64 ; for test-time-aware baselines that naturally benefit from larger candidate sets, we also report m = 128 m=128 compute-unmatched tests. We construct disjoint training, validation, and held-out evaluation prompt sets. For the comprehensive baseline comparison, we use core250 , a pre-specified 250-prompt held-out set on which we evaluate the full baseline suite. We additionally report results on core500 , a larger 500-prompt held-out set containing core250, for larger-scale confirmation of the key methods. The default training configuration uses rollout group size m = 64 m=64 , KL coefficient β = 0.1  eta=0.1 , learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and 450 training steps. Checkpoints are selected using the same validation rule for all methods. For scaling experiments, we sample 512 512 completions per prompt to evaluate up to N = 512 N=512 . We report confidence intervals by paired prompt bootstrap. To address the practical budget-mismatch regime m ≪ N m\ll N , we used test-time scaling-law structure to approximate the best-of- N N policy gradient from a small rollout group, leading to Tail-Extrapolated Advantage (TEA) and its fixed-order debiased variant, Prefix-TEA. We provided finite-sample error and post-training guarantees, and showed empirically that these estimators improve best-of- N N performance over standard and test-time-aware baselines across datasets, reward models, and budget settings. This work also opens up a number of directions for future research. • We use a Gaussian upper-tail approximation to derive TEA and Prefix-TEA, but other tail structures could be used to construct different extrapolated estimators. In particular, it is interesting to explore methods that adapt to any tail structure, rather than relying on a fixed parametric form. Moreover, it is an important future direction to extend the idea to non-smooth reward distributions, such as zero-one rewards in the pass@ k k setting. • It is useful to extend the methods to other test-time strategies beyond best-of- N N , such as tree search methods, self-refine procedures, or interaction with external tools. In general, the tail-extrapolation principle applies to any test-time strategy that admits a scaling-law structure, but the specific form of the estimator and the training procedure may need to be adapted to the strategy and its scaling law. In Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing , pages 5642–5665, 2025. Appendix A Additional related work Single-response post-training. Most LLM post-training methods are designed to improve the quality of a single sampled response. Reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) fine-tunes a policy against a learned reward model, typically with a KL penalty to keep the policy close to a reference model [ 13 ] . Preference-optimization methods such as DPO optimize an equivalent preference objective without explicitly running online RL [ 15 ] , while grouped policy-gradient methods such as GRPO improve the efficiency of RL-style post-training by normalizing rewards within a rollout group [ 19 ] . These methods are natural when the deployed model returns one response, but they do not directly optimize the multi-candidate behavior used by test-time strategies such as best-of- N N . This distinction is practically important because post-training changes not only the average quality of responses, but also the distribution of candidate responses at test time. Empirical studies show that RLHF, instruction tuning, and reward-based fine-tuning can reduce the diversity of generated candidates [ 9 , 14 ] . Complementary theory shows that reward variation also matters for optimization: if a reward model induces too little variance under the current policy, the RLHF objective can become flat and slow to optimize [ 16 ] . These works motivate a distributional view of post-training, but they do not specify how to optimize a target best-of- N N deployment objective. Test-time strategies and test-time scaling. A separate line of work improves language model performance by spending more compute at deployment. Verifier-based methods generate many candidate solutions and return the one ranked highest by a verifier [ 6 ] . Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and aggregates their final answers [ 24 ] . Repeated-sampling studies show that coverage can increase predictably with the number of attempts, especially when candidate solutions can be automatically checked [ 4 ] . More broadly, test-time compute has become an independent scaling axis: it can be allocated to search, verifier scoring, adaptive procedures, or even problem-specific test-time training, and has been used to surpass prior human-engineered or best-known solutions in discovery-style tasks [ 20 , 25 , 11 ] . These results make the budget mismatch especially important. At deployment, one may spend a large amount of compute on a single hard prompt to find one exceptional response; during post-training, the same per-prompt budget is usually infeasible because optimization must cover many prompts. Best-of- N N is one of the simplest and most widely used instances of this principle. BoNBoN studies the best-of- N N distribution itself, relates it to KL-regularized alignment, and trains a model to mimic this distribution so that the sampling cost can be amortized [ 8 ] . Closest to our test-time scaling perspective, prior work shows that best-of- N N scaling laws can be predicted from m ≪ N m\ll N samples by extrapolating the upper tail of the reward distribution [ 10 ] . Our work uses the same high-level idea for a different purpose: rather than predicting the value of best-of- N N inference or amortizing its output distribution, we use tail extrapolation to construct a policy-gradient estimator for improving best-of- N N performance. Test-time-aware post-training. Recent work directly adapts post-training to the deployment-time procedure. Best-of- N N -aware imitation-learning and RL objectives have been introduced [ 5 ] . Generic k k -sample test-time objectives, including pass@ k k and majority vote, have also been optimized [ 22 ] . Low-variance unbiased estimators have been derived for pass@ k k and its gradient [ 23 ] , and RL has been aligned with best-of- N N sampling through max@ k k optimization [ 1 ] . More general frameworks also show that alignment should depend on the test-time rule: InfAlign derives procedure-dependent reward transformations [ 3 ] , and Compute Aligned Training views te
